data.body: Patients across Great Britain will continue to have access to the medical devices and in vitro diagnostic devices (IVDs) they rely on, from insulin pumps and replacement joints to diagnostic tests and surgical equipment, after the government has today, 21 October 2026, confirmed it will continue to accept CE marked medical devices on a long-term basis. The decision follows a public consultation , which ran from 16 February 2026 to 10 April 2026, that received more than 1,000 responses from patients, healthcare organisations, industry and others. The decision means the UK will not require an additional approval route for devices already approved for the EU market, avoiding duplication for manufacturers and helping to maintain stable supply and patient access to medical technologies. More than 90% of medical devices registered for use in Great Britain currently carry a CE mark, meaning they have been assessed and approved for the European market, and this approval has been recognised to provide access to the Great British market. Continuing to recognise these devices will help maintain safe, uninterrupted access to the treatments and technologies that patients and the NHS rely on. This sits alongside the UKCA marking route, which continues to operate as the domestic approval pathway for devices placed on the market in Great Britain. These arrangements sit alongside strengthened post-market surveillance and reporting requirements already in place. The MHRA will continue to oversee all devices on the UK market, monitor safety through mechanisms including the Yellow Card scheme, and work closely with international partners to share safety information enabling the MHRA to take action to protect patients where needed. In parallel, the UKCA route remains the current domestic approval route for medical devices placed on the market in Great Britain. This is being modernised through the pre-market statutory instrument, which will update the requirements devices must meet to be UKCA marked. Alongside this, we will continue to seek enabling powers through primary legislation to develop a future licencing approach for medical devices, intended to support a more modern and adaptable framework that is better able to respond to advancing medical technologies, including software and AI medical devices, reflecting recommendations from the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare. Our approach will secure supply of medical devices for UK patients while also supporting safe, rapid access to innovation so that patients can benefit from the best new technologies. By providing a clear and predictable regulatory framework. The approach supports the development and availability of new health technologies for patients, in line with the ambitions of the Government’s Life Sciences Sector Plan and 10 Year Health Plan. Continued recognition of CE-marked devices also reflects the wider ambition of the MHRA’s 2030 Strategy to expand reliance and recognition routes with trusted regulators, reducing regulatory burden, strengthen supply resilience and supporting timely patient access. Lawrence Tallon, Chief Executive of the MHRA, said: “This decision gives patients, the NHS and industry the long-term certainty they need on access to medical devices. data.body: Commitments made in the strategy will enable the regulator to keep pace with rapid advances in science, technology and personalised healthcare, to benefit patients, and position the UK as a leading place to develop, launch and use new medicines and technologies safely and effectively. By 2030 , the MHRA aims to be even more patient-centred, support patients having faster access to safe, effective treatments, and have more data-connectivity and global influence. The strategy defines the MHRA’s mission to contribute to ‘health and prosperity for all, through scientific excellence’ and reaffirms its central purpose to protect patients, improve public health and enable faster access to innovation. Minister for Health Innovation, James Frith said: We want patients to benefit faster from the latest medicines and technologies, while maintaining the highest standards of safety. This strategy will help the MHRA keep pace with the latest innovations in AI, data and medicine, while strengthening its ability to crack down on illegal medicines to keep the public safe. This will put patients at the heart of regulation, whoever they are and wherever they live — with greater diversity in clinical studies and a Women’s Health Plan to secure better outcomes for women. MHRA Chief Executive, Lawrence Tallon said: We are in the midst of a period of extraordinary scientific and technological discovery, which is helping to reshape how diseases can be prevented, diagnosed and treated. AI is transforming both regulated products and how organisations are run. Cell and gene therapies are offering the possibility of long-lasting or curative treatments. Precision and personalised medicines are transforming the accuracy and effectiveness of treatments. Advanced diagnostics are driving earlier intervention and better outcomes for patients. These ground-breaking developments challenge traditional regulatory models and require innovative approaches to evidence generation, clinical research design, manufacturing oversight and safety and surveillance. Our 2030 Strategy sets out how, working with our partners across health and life sciences, we will translate scientific and technological innovation into better health outcomes for people across all four nations of the UK. MHRA Chair, Professor Anthony Harnden said: Our 2030 Strategy sets out our vision for how we will harness extraordinary scientific and technological advances to catalyse innovation in the life sciences and accelerate access to safe and effective treatments for patients. This is an ambition we can only achieve by working together, and I would like to thank patients, healthcare professionals, the life sciences industry and our international counterparts for their continued collaboration and shared commitment to protecting the public. Richard Torbett, Chief Executive of the ABPI, said: In 2024, our industry set out a clear ambition for the MHRA: to be among the best in the world at both regulating innovation and innovating regulation. This strategy matches that ambition and, in many areas, goes further. The MHRA’s new strategy is clear on speed, clear on standards and clear on how performance will be measured, with firm service guarantees, closer working with NICE and patients at the centre of every decision. The agency has already made real progress on these issues, and this strategy builds on that progress with confidence. We look forward to working with the MHRA to turn ambition into delivery, so that…
data.brief: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has set out ambitious plans to translate cutting-edge scientific and technological innovation into better health outcomes for patients across all four nations of the UK, in its 2030 Strategy published today.

data.body: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is introducing a series of new measures to strengthen how key risks associated with antidepressant medicines are communicated to patients, carers and healthcare professionals. The changes follow an extensive review initiated by the Commission on Human Medicines (CHM), in response to concerns raised by both patients and families about how information on two key areas is communicated in patient information leaflets. These are suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and sexual dysfunction that continues after treatment is stopped. Throughout the review we engaged directly with patients and families and considered the latest available evidence and expert clinical advice. Dr Alison Cave, MHRA Chief Safety Officer, said: “Patients need clear and accessible information about the benefits and risks of medicines so they can make informed decisions. “We are incredibly grateful for the valuable contributions of patients, families, clinicians and experts to this review. “These measures will help ensure patients, carers and healthcare professionals can have more informed conversations about the benefits and risks associated with antidepressant medicines, and better support people throughout their treatment.” “Antidepressants are effective medicines for the treatment of depression and other conditions. When used appropriately and under clinical supervision, for the vast majority of individuals, the benefits outweigh the risks. The aim is not to discourage use, but to improve the prominence and clarity of the existing warnings. “It’s imperative that patients do not stop taking these medicines without first speaking to their healthcare professional.” As a result of this review, patient information leaflets for antidepressants will be updated, including a new boxed warning signposting to information on suicidal thoughts and behaviours, making information easier to find. The expectation is that a new patient card will be included in or on the medicine box to reinforce key safety messaging and help patients and carers understand how and when to get further support. Patient information leaflets for certain antidepressants will be updated to include the term ‘Post SSRI Sexual Dysfunction’ (PSSD), to explain the risk of symptoms continuing after stopping treatment. This update aims to better reflect patient experiences and existing safety information. Finally, a supporting safety (ancillary) leaflet is being developed by the MHRA with the wider healthcare system, which will be given to patients at their first appointment discussing antidepressants. It will describe the key risks and benefits to support informed decision making about their treatment. This safety leaflet will also be given to patients who are already receiving antidepressants. This will be available in 2027. Chris Bird, programme manager for patient safety at NICE, said: “This review will ensure patients and healthcare professionals have the most up to date information to help them make crucial decisions on treatment and support. “We are grateful to have collaborated with the MHRA on the review, with NICE colleagues joining its expert working group. “As with all new safety advice issued from the MHRA, we will consider the implications of this advice on published NICE guidance and review our recommendations if required.” We will continue to work with partners across the healthcare system to support more consistent communication of risks…

data.summary: A Shanghai court confirmed the criminal conviction of Wang Jianyang, one of the operators of pirate streaming platform Aiyifan. The court also refused to transfer Aiyifan’s domains, noting that the sites carry content from other rightsholders too. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Chinese Court Jails Aiyifan Operator, U.S. Judge Won’t Transfer Pirate Site’s Domains

data.summary: VPN providers and Cloudflare only have to make a reasonable effort to block pirate sports streams in France. That's the conclusion of two Paris court rulings that refused beIN Sports' request for penalties of €10,000 per day, per domain. Meanwhile, the Paris Court of Appeal put a separate VPN blocking appeal on hold until France's Supreme Court rules on DNS blocking. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: VPNs and Cloudflare Escape beIN’s €10,000-a-Day Piracy Blocking Penalties

data.summary: The RIAA has submitted its latest overview of "notorious markets" to the U.S. Government. It lists familiar names such as The Pirate Bay and Rapidgator, but the music group also flags shadow library Anna's Archive and AI voice-cloning service Lalals. The RIAA presents both as "additional" areas of concern, not as official watchlist candidates. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: RIAA Flags Anna’s Archive and AI Voice Cloner to U.S. Government

data.summary: A group of major publishers has asked a New York federal court to issue a $19.5 million default judgment against pirate library WeLib. The site allegedly copied its code and most of its collection from Anna's Archive, which lost a nearly identical case in May. Ironically, the publishers' brief appears to 'copy' from Anna's Archive as well, or at least from their own lawsuit against the shadow library. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Publishers Seek $19.5m From Pirate Library WeLib, Recycle Anna’s Archive Claims

data.summary: When pirate streaming giant Cineby shut down at the end of August, its operators blamed the loss of their main video providers. Now, the MPA informs the U.S. Trade Representative that the site stopped operating following "MPA and ACE actions," adding that the same applies to anime piracy portal AnimeFLV. At the same time, the MPA flags several persistent piracy threats, including Telegram, Kisskh, and MagisTV. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: MPA Takes Credit for Shutting Down Piracy Giants AnimeFLV and Cineby

data.summary: The Entertainment Software Association has asked the U.S. Government to label the Denuvo cracker ‘voices38’ as a notorious piracy market. The game industry group argues that the cracker is an essential source in the game piracy ecosystem, feeding repackers and torrent sites. A notorious market flag is no guarantee of success, however, as FitGirl's previous listings show. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Game Industry Asks U.S. to Flag Denuvo Cracker ‘voices38’ as Notorious Piracy Threat

data.summary: In recent years, AI has made it much easier to create new websites and tools. That also applies to pirate sites, including TorrentClaw, a torrent search engine that’s largely built with AI. The site's TrueSpec feature, for example, checks what’s inside torrents. The results reveal a recurring malware trick, where a genuine VLC player is used as a decoy to load a malicious file. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: AI-Built Torrent Site Looks Inside Downloads to Catch Fakes and Malware

data.summary: The .ly domain of Spanish pirate streaming portal Series.ly was suspended by its Libyan registrar this week, more than a week after a Madrid court approved a broad anti-piracy order against the site. Soon after the domain was lost the Telegram and Discord were rebranded to Cinubo. The Spanish order also covers future mirrors, however, so whether this will apply to Cinubo has yet to be seen. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Pirate Streaming Portal Series.ly Has Domain Suspended, Rebrand Surfaces (Updated)

data.summary: Cloudflare doesn't block pirate sports streaming sites through its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver in France, only through its CDN. The Paris Judicial Court has now accepted that stance, rejecting Canal+'s request for penalties of €50,000 per site, per day. Interestingly, the court's conclusion relies on statistics provided by Canal+ itself. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Cloudflare Keeps 1.1.1.1 Out of Piracy Blocking, Escapes Penalties in France

data.summary: Pirate streaming app MovieBox has been downloaded more than 300 million times from Palm Store, the app store that's preinstalled on Tecno, Infinix and itel phones. This is a thorn in the side of rightsholders, which have flagged the app to the European Commission. French pay-TV group Canal+ goes a step further, linking the operation to smartphone maker Transsion. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Pirate App MovieBox Passes 300 Million Downloads as Rightsholders Alert EU

data.summary: Denuvo has asked a California federal court for permission to subpoena Discord, Valve and Reddit, hoping to unmask the anonymous game cracker 'voices38.' The anti-piracy company wants account details, IP addresses and Steam transaction histories tied to a Discord ID, a Reddit account and seven Steam profiles. The filing also reveals that Denuvo uncovered cryptocurrency transactions by the cracker on the exchange FixedFloat. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Denuvo Asks Court to Unmask Game Cracker ‘voices38’, Reveals Crypto Transactions

data.summary: DNS resolver Quad9 is considering pulling out of France after broadcaster beIN Sports asked a Paris court to impose non-compliance penalties that could go up to €580,000 per day. The Swiss non-profit is not blocking the pirate tennis streams covered by a May site-blocking order, arguing that it can't reliably limit the blocks to French users. A decision is expected later this month. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: DNS Resolver Quad9 Rejects French Piracy Blocks, Weighs Exit as beIN Seeks Up to €580K a Day

data.summary: The two competing pirate site-blocking bills that were introduced in Congress recently take different approaches. While Rep. Darrell Issa's ACPA targets VPNs and provides broad liability protections to Internet service providers, the bipartisan and bicameral DEFEND IP Act explicitly excludes VPNs, while covering more smaller ISPs. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Two U.S. Site-Blocking Bills Compete Over VPN Rules and ISP Liability

data.summary: An alleged operator of pirate IPTV services Kemo IPTV and Lemo TV faces criminal prosecution in Dubai, following a complaint from anti-piracy coalition ACE. The case surprisingly surfaced in a Florida federal court, where DISH Network's request for a $28.65 million default judgment against the same defendants was just denied. According to the judge, DISH failed to show that they were properly served. From: TF , for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.
data.title: Alleged Kemo IPTV Operator Faces Criminal Prosecution in Dubai Following ACE Complaint
